Can the IRS survive these seven major hurdles?

By Daniel Hood
About Daniel
twitter
accountingedit

daniel.hood@arizent.com
linkedin
daniel-hood-3494ab49
Published October 26, 2026 7:33 PM
|
Updated October 26, 2026 10:00 PM
1 Min Read
  • Facebook
  • Twitter
  • LinkedIn
  • Email

Sponsored by
0:00 / 0:45
Instaread

The Internal Revenue Service faces seven major challenges in the coming fiscal year, according to a new report — and while it is making headway in some areas, a scarcity of resources is making them all difficult to address.

The new report from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration summarizes the most significant management and performance challenges faced by the IRS, along with the agency's progress on them, and which of TIGTA's recommendations the IRS has implemented.

The seven, in no particular order, are listed below.

Managing resources

Luis A. Orozco/Cin8 - stock.adobe.com
With its staff having been cut by 30% last year, and its budget by 20%, the IRS is being pushed to do much more with much less — and even when it is given money to hire new employees, TIGTA pointed out, it faces hiring process delays.

With all that, the report said the IRS is making some progress with backfilling open positions, streamlining tax processing with technology, and cross-training employees.

Improving operational efficiencies

Jeff Fusco/Getty Images
With the Trump administration mandating electronic payments instead of checks, and pushing for an end to remote work, the agency is under pressure to make major changes in how it operates.

TIGTA said the IRS is making some progress — particularly in using artificial intelligence to create efficiencies, but still has some work to do.

Protecting taxpayer data

Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg
Given the vast amount of taxpayer information the IRS collects, and the wide array of different systems of different ages that it keeps all that data in, it should come as no surprise that keeping it all safe is a serious challenge.

The inspector general report noted a number of issues here — such as IRS employees retaining access to data long after they were no longer entitled to it, and insufficient controls over contractor sites — as well as the agency's inability to determine which other federal agencies it had data-sharing agreements with, and whether those partners were protecting the data. In particular, it noted the Immigration and Customs Enforcement unit of the Department of Homeland Security did not meet safeguarding standards.

Implementing tax law changes

Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg
The late passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act had the IRS scrambling to come up with guidance, forms and submission processing and compliance controls, but TIGTA said it was generally successful.

The inspector general did note, however, a few shortfalls in guidance and controls, which it will be keeping an eye on.

Improving taxpayer service and protecting taxpayers' rights

Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg
Here, TIGTA was primarily concerned with the IRS's shortcomings in terms of the knowledge and professionalism of its phone representatives, as well as the limits of the chatbot applications it uses.

In addition, victims of identity theft continue to face lengthy delays — mostly because they are waiting a long time for an IRS assistor to become available.

Modernizing information technology

Jaque Da Silva/Rafael Henrique - stock.adobe.com
Bringing the IRS's massive tech stack up to date has been a problem for decades, but it is making more concerted efforts of late to replace old legacy systems, to expand its use of AI, and to implement its new filing system, IRIS.

As it's doing that, though, TIGTA suggested that it's not adequately managing all the security aspects of the transition and its new systems.

Ensuring tax compliance

Natasa Adzic/stock.adobe.com
In the end, all of these hurdles combined impede the IRS's ability to fulfill on its main mission: ensuring taxpayers are complying with the Tax Code. Audit rates are dropping, and of those audits that actually occur, many result in no change — which suggests the agency needs to refine how it picks cases to examine. Furthermore, it's estimated that over a quarter (26.5%) of payments in the IRS's four high-risk programs are improper.

TIGTA said the IRS has made some progress in preventing fraud and protecting revenue, but the sums involved have been relatively small compared to the amount of improper payments made, and of the overall Tax Gap.
